questions.stem: A 42-year-old man was admitted with a 2-day history of progressive dyspnea and a one-week history of fever, chills, and productive cough. The patient eventually required intubation and mechanical ventilation due to respiratory distress and hypoxemia. A chest radiograph demonstrated consolidation in the left and right lower lobes and patchy airspace opacity in the right middle lobe. Blood cultures were taken and empirical antimicrobials started.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate further investigation?

options.text: Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae urine antigen assays
NAAT for Chlamydia and Mycoplasma pneumoniae on throat swab

questions.explanation: Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae urine antigen assays The patient in this clinical vignette has presented with a severe pneumonia requiring admission to the intensive care unit for mechanical ventilation. The recommendation for patients presenting with a severe community-acquired pneumonia is to have Legionella and S. pneumoniae urine antigen testing in addition to blood and sputum cultures.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q13

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man was admitted with a 1-week history of nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, dry cough, fever, chills, and myalgia. He was beginning to feel better until 48 hours ago when he developed recurrence of fever and chills, a productive cough with blood-streaked sputum, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. On physical examination, his temperature was 38.8°C, blood pressure 100/50 mmHg, pulse rate 110/minute, and respiration rate 24/minute. CXR: right middle lobe airspace disease with a small area of cavitation as well as blunting of the right costophrenic angle.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and azithromycin This patient has a classic presentation for a postinfluenza or viral illness with initial flu-like symptoms progressing to worsening fever, productive cough, and imaging findings suggestive of a pleural effusion. Although the infection could be due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, there is concern for postinfluenza Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia, and the patient requires empiric coverage for MRSA. Although daptomycin does provide MRSA coverage, it is inactivated in the lung by surfactant and would be a poor choice in this clinical scenario.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q5

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with no past medical history presented with 3 days of fever and cough. She had no known allergies. On exam her temperature was 39.1°C. Investigations: CXR: patchy bilateral infiltrates
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone and azithromycin The patient presents in the setting of community-acquired pneumonia. The only answer choice with a guideline-recommended regimen for CAP is ceftriaxone and azithromycin. The patient has no past medical history or risk factors warranting pseudomonal coverage and does not present with evidence of a pleural effusion after a viral illness that would be concerning for MRSA infection.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q5

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman was diagnosed with healthcareassociated pneumonia. She was a nursing home resident with no drug allergies, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and acute on chronic kidney disease. Investigations: Creatinine clearance 25 mL/min (baseline creatinine clearance 40 mL/min) Sputum culture negative Multiplex PCR respiratory virus panel negative
questions.lead_in: What antipseudomonal agent poses the greatest risk for neurotoxicity?
questions.explanation: Cefepime While each of the beta-lactam antibiotics listed has the potential to cause neurotoxicity, cefepime is most associated with the development of this adverse effect. A US Food and Drug Administration safety alert for cefepime identified age >50 and inadequate renal dosing adjustments as risk factors for neurotoxicity.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q4

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital with a 2-day history of fever and chills, dyspnea, and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Five months earlier she underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for myelodysplastic syndrome. She was taking trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, aciclovir, prednisone, and cyclosporine. Investigations: CXR: infiltrate in the left lower lobe
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae The patient is 5 months out from a stem cell transplant and presents with a lobar pneumonia. Although she is immunocompromised, she is on Pneumocystis prophylaxis and does not present with interstitial lung disease. CMV pneumonia would also be unlikely without a diffuse pneumonitis on imaging, and she would require histopathology with positive CMV staining to make the diagnosis. RSV pneumonia would normally present with bilateral asymmetric infiltrates and Candida spp. rarely cause pneumonia. The correct answer is therefore pneumococcal pneumonia as this patient is at risk for pneumococcal pneumonia, and a lower lobe infiltrate would fit the classic description.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q4

questions.question: A patient is admitted with a community-acquired pneumonia. The culture reveals MRSA, resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and macrolides. The patient had an allergic reaction to vancomycin. He is started on daptomycin but keeps worsening clinically.
questions.question_raw: 11. A patient is admitted with a community-acquired pneumonia. The culture reveals an MRSA, resistant to TMP-SMX and macrolides. The patient had an allergic reaction to vancomycin. He is started on daptomycin, but keeps worsening clinically.

parts.text: Why is he still worsening?
What are two antibiotics you could use in this particular scenario (assuming the organism is susceptible)?

parts_raw.text: Why is he still worsening?
b) What are 2 antibiotics you could use in this particular scenario (assuming the organism is susceptible)?

questions.model_answer: a) Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant, so it does not achieve effective bactericidal concentrations in the alveoli and is ineffective for pneumonia. b) (1) Linezolid; (2) Ceftaroline. (Other acceptable MRSA pneumonia options include telavancin.)

cohort_answer.text: Daptomycin is not active in the lung (inactivated by pulmonary surfactant).

questions.question: A pregnant woman is admitted with mild community-acquired pneumonia and has a history of Stevens-Johnson syndrome to penicillin. What is your treatment?
questions.question_raw: Pneumonia (inpatient, mild) in a pregnant woman with SJ to PCN.

parts.text: What is your treatment?

parts_raw.text: What is your treatment.

questions.model_answer: Avoid ALL beta-lactams (including cephalosporins and carbapenems) given the Stevens-Johnson reaction. Give a macrolide, azithromycin (safe in pregnancy, covers atypicals and many pneumococci), combined with clindamycin for typical gram-positive (S. pneumoniae, S. aureus) coverage; add aztreonam if gram-negative coverage is required. Avoid fluoroquinolones and doxycycline in pregnancy if alternatives exist.
questions.beyond_mandell: Chapter gives the beta-lactam-allergy ICU regimen (respiratory fluoroquinolone +/- clindamycin) but not pregnancy-specific choices; regimen based on CAP guidance plus pregnancy safety (macrolides safe, quinolones/doxycycline avoided).

cohort_answer.text: Macrolides are safe for pregnancy. UpToDate suggests: Clindamycin plus aztreonam for mild CAP requiring admission with contraindication to cephalosporins. Short course of Moxifloxacin should be fine (author's opinion). If severe: Vancomycin, aztreonam and azithromycin. (ATS 2001; note - avoid all beta-lactams if Stevens-Johnson syndrome.)

questions.question: Empiric treatment of community-acquired pneumonia in a pregnant woman with a penicillin allergy.

parts.text: A woman is 16 weeks pregnant. She is admitted for community-acquired pneumonia. She has Stevens-Johnson syndrome to penicillin. She is tachypneic but otherwise stable. What is one empiric regimen that you would recommend to treat her pneumonia?

parts_raw.text: A woman is 16 weeks pregnant. She is admitted for community acquired pneumonia. She has SJS to penicillin. She is tachypneic but otherwise stable. What is one empiric regimen that you would recommend to treat her pneumonia?

questions.model_answer: One regimen: azithromycin plus clindamycin. This avoids all beta-lactams (mandatory with Stevens-Johnson syndrome), is safe in pregnancy, and covers atypical pathogens (azithromycin) plus typical gram-positives including S. pneumoniae and S. aureus (clindamycin). Add aztreonam if gram-negative coverage is needed; avoid fluoroquinolones and doxycycline in pregnancy where possible.
questions.beyond_mandell: Pregnancy-specific regimen not in chapter; based on CAP guidance plus pregnancy drug-safety (macrolides safe; beta-lactams contraindicated after SJS).

questions.question: You use high-dose amoxicillin 1000 mg PO TID for uncomplicated bacterial pneumonia.
questions.question_raw: You use high dose Amoxicillin 1000 mg po TID for uncomplicated bacterial pneumonia, what are:

parts.text: pathogen-specific reasons for doing so
the mechanistic reasons for doing so

parts_raw.text: pathogen-specific reasons for doing so
the mechanistic reasons for doing so

questions.model_answer: a) Pathogen-specific: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the predominant pathogen, and rising penicillin MICs (drug-resistant S. pneumoniae, favoured by prior antibiotic use/long-term care) mean higher amoxicillin doses are needed to overcome reduced-susceptibility strains; high-dose amoxicillin is the recommended oral beta-lactam where DRSP risk applies. b) Mechanistic: beta-lactams are time-dependent killers, so efficacy depends on the free drug level exceeding the MIC for ~40-50% of the dosing interval; raising the dose increases the time above MIC and optimizes pharmacodynamic target attainment against higher-MIC pneumococci.

cohort_answer.text:
a) Increasing MICs of Strep pneumonia requiring higher doses
b) Improve time above MIC?

questions.question: For each of the following conditions, list the shortest effective duration of antibiotics: retropharyngeal abscess (pediatric), ventilator-associated pneumonia (adult), community-acquired pneumonia, cellulitis, and uncomplicated pyelonephritis.
questions.question_raw: For the following conditions, list the shortest effective duration of antibiotics: Retropharyngeal abscess on Peds exam, VAP on adult exam, CAP, Cellulitis, Uncomplicated pyelonephritis.

parts.text: For each condition, list the shortest effective duration of antibiotics.

parts_raw.text: For each condition, list the shortest effective duration of antibiotics.

questions.model_answer: (1) Retropharyngeal abscess (peds): ~14 days total (with surgical drainage as needed). (2) VAP: 7 days. (3) CAP: 5 days (minimum, provided clinically stable/afebrile 48-72 h). (4) Cellulitis: 5 days (uncomplicated, extend if not improving). (5) Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 7 days (fluoroquinolone, e.g. ciprofloxacin; levofloxacin 750 mg can be 5 days where local resistance <10%).
questions.beyond_mandell: Durations are not specified in this chapter; from IDSA/ATS CAP (2019), IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP (2016), IDSA SSTI (2014) and IDSA uncomplicated cystitis/pyelonephritis (2011) guidelines.

cohort_answer.text: Retropharyngeal abscess 14 days (UTD, Redbook); VAP 7 days; CAP 5 days; Cellulitis 5 days; Uncomplicated pyelo 7 days. Resource: AMMI Duration Paper https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9615468/

questions.model_answer: a) VAP: 7 days. b) CAP: 5 days (minimum, once afebrile and clinically stable 48-72 h). c) Cellulitis: 5 days (uncomplicated). d) Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 7 days with a fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg for 5 days where local resistance <10%; 10-14 days for beta-lactams/TMP-SMX).

questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort's 3-day durations for VAP and CAP are not guideline-endorsed: IDSA/ATS recommend 7 days for VAP and a minimum of 5 days for CAP.

cohort_answer.text: VAP: 3 days (IDSA 2016). CAP: 3 days (IDSA 2019). Cellulitis: 5 days (IDSA 2014). Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 5 days (IDSA 2010; fluoroquinolones only for 5d if local resistance <10%).

questions.question: Based on the best available evidence, what is the shortest available duration of therapy for each of the following conditions, assuming clinical improvement and defervescence at 48 hours on therapy in each case?
questions.question_raw: Based on the best available evidence, what is the shortest available duration of therapy for the following conditions, assuming clinical improvement and defervesced at 48 hours in each case on therapy?

parts.text: Uncomplicated, fully-susceptible Escherichia coli pyelonephritis without any stones or obstruction.
Klebsiella bacteremia due to a now-passed stone with no evidence of abscess or complication.
Fully-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis without dissemination.
Hospital-acquired Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with line removal, repeat blood cultures negative at 48 hours, TEE negative for infective endocarditis, and no other signs of metastatic infection.
Community-acquired pneumonia without a microbiologic diagnosis, not on oxygen.
Perforated diverticulitis status post OR washout with no concern of residual abscess per the surgeon.

parts_raw.text: Uncomplicated, fully-susceptible E coli pyelonephritis without any stones or obstruction?
Klebsiella bacteremia due to a now-passed stone with no evidence of abscess or complication?
Fully-susceptible, pulmonary TB without dissemination?
Hospital-acquired S. aureus bacteremia with line removal, repeat blood cultures at 48 hours negative, TEE negative for IE, and no other signs of metastatic infection?
Community acquired pneumonia without microbiologic diagnosis not on oxygen?
Perforated diverticulitis status post OR for washout without any concern of residual abscess per the surgeon?

questions.model_answer: a) 7 days (fluoroquinolone; ceftriaxone/oral beta-lactam course 10-14 days, but shortest evidence-based fluoroquinolone course is 7 days). b) 7 days: source-controlled uncomplicated gram-negative bacteremia is non-inferior at 7 vs 14 days (Yahav/von Dach trials). c) 6 months: 2 months RIPE intensive phase then 4 months rifampin/isoniazid continuation. d) 14 days from the first negative blood culture: uncomplicated catheter-associated SAB qualifies for a 14-day course when the focus is removed, endocarditis is excluded, follow-up cultures are negative, fever resolves by 72 h, and no metastatic foci are present. e) 5 days: minimum for CAP if clinically stable and afebrile 48-72 h. f) 4 days after adequate source control (STOP-IT trial).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the S. aureus bacteremia duration is from this chapter (p. 2426); the pyelonephritis (7 d FQ), gram-negative bacteremia (7 d, Yahav 2019/von Dach 2020), TB (6 mo, ATS/CDC/PHAC), CAP (5 d, ATS/IDSA), and diverticulitis (4 d post-source-control, STOP-IT/Sawyer 2015) durations rest on those trials/guidelines, not on Mandell ch. 194.

questions.question_raw: Curve which showed three curves representing different AUC/MIC ratios used, % of isolates remaining susceptible / days of clinical infection

parts.text: State which ratio (AUC/MIC < 100 or AUC/MIC ≥ 100) is represented by the bottom (dotted) curve, and explain.
Name two classes of antimicrobials whose efficacy is predicted by AUC/MIC.
Give three principles to reduce drug resistance when treating a patient with gram-negative pneumonia in the ICU.

parts_raw.text: A. Asked to state which ratio (AUC/MIC < 100 or AUC/MIC >= 100) was represented by the bottom curve (in the graph below, the dotted curve) and explain.
B. Two classes of antimicrobials whose efficacy is predicted by AUC/MIC.
C. Three principles to reduce drug resistance when treating a patient with gram-negative pneumonia in ICU.

questions.model_answer: a) The lower (dotted) curve represents AUC/MIC < 100: a sub-target AUC/MIC fails to achieve concentration-dependent killing, so susceptibility is lost more rapidly and resistance emerges — an AUC/MIC ≥ 100-125 is needed to maximize killing and suppress resistant subpopulations. b) (1) Fluoroquinolones. (2) Aminoglycosides (glycopeptides/vancomycin are also AUC/MIC-driven). c) (1) Choose empiric therapy guided by the local antibiogram and dose to achieve PK/PD targets. (2) De-escalate to the narrowest effective agent and limit duration (~7 days for VAP). (3) Apply infection-control measures and therapeutic drug monitoring to prevent selection/transmission of resistant organisms.
questions.beyond_mandell: AUC/MIC pharmacodynamic relationships are from Mandell's antimicrobial pharmacodynamics chapter and VAP/HAP management guidance, not the stewardship text read.

cohort_answer.text:
[image-based question: graph of AUC/MIC curves not otherwise described]. Concentration-Dependent Killing: rate/extent of killing increases with peak drug concentration; usually protein or DNA synthesis inhibitors e.g. Aminoglycosides, Fluoroquinolones, Daptomycin; exhibit post-antibiotic effect. Time-Dependent Killing: usually cell wall synthesis inhibitors e.g. Beta-lactams, Clindamycin, Macrolides, probably Vancomycin; bactericidal activity continues as long as plasma concentration > MIC
Glycopeptides; Tetracyclines; Oxazolidinones; Azithromycin; Triazoles; Clindamycin
Base choice of antibiotics on local antibiogram; Shorten duration - 5-7 days for VAP; Use therapeutic drug monitoring; Implement protocols. Additional: Empiric treatment informed by local antibiogram; dosing based on PK/PD data; definitive therapy based on susceptibility testing; optimize duration to 7 days; appropriate infection control practices

questions.question: A 3-year-old girl has a URTI followed by fever and respiratory distress. Chest radiograph shows a large lobar consolidation and a pleural effusion.
questions.question_raw: 3 year old girl with URTI followed by fever and respiratory distress. CXR shows a large lobar consolidation and pleural effusion.

parts.text: List the 3 most likely organisms to cause this.
What other information do you want to know?
What is your treatment?
What other management might be helpful?

parts_raw.text: A) List the 3 most likely organisms to cause this?
B) What other information do you want to know?
C) What is your treatment?
D) What other management might be helpful?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common cause of lobar pneumonia; large effusions support a bacterial cause). (2) Staphylococcus aureus (necrosis, pneumatoceles, empyema in children). (3) Streptococcus pyogenes/Group A streptococcus (beta-hemolytic streptococci carry the highest rate of pleural involvement; H. influenzae is a further consideration). b) Immunization status (PCV, Hib); severity/vital signs and oxygenation; recent influenza/viral prodrome; MRSA risk and colonization; sick contacts; recurrent infections suggesting immune defect; and pleural fluid analysis (pH, glucose, LDH, Gram stain/culture) to define whether drainage is needed. c) Empiric coverage for S. pneumoniae (high-dose ampicillin, or ceftriaxone/cefotaxime per local susceptibility), ADDING vancomycin if severe or MRSA is suspected/proven. d) Drain the pleural effusion/empyema: complicated effusions (pH <7.2, positive culture) and pus mandate drainage, which speeds resolution; obtain fluid for culture as it can yield the etiologic diagnosis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Pediatric-specific empiric drug choices/doses follow PIDS/IDSA pediatric CAP guidance (2011); chapter Table 67.5 is adult-oriented.

cohort_answer.text:
Streptococcus pneumoniae; Staphylococcus aureus; Group A streptococcus; Haemophilus influenzae; Moraxella catarrhalis
Vaccination status; recurrent sinopulmonary infections; close contacts (need for chemoprophylaxis); MRSA colonization rate (personal/family)
Amp or Cefotaxime/CTX based on local guidelines + Vanco if proven or severe suspected MRSA pneumonia
Drain pleural effusion to expedite resolution of symptoms and complex pneumonia
